solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Diarist has a furtive look, they say

indicators.note: a report of what people say signals that the word is judged by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: someone who sneaks a glance peeps

explanation.surface: Someone keeping a journal glances about shiftily, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Pepys, the 17th-century London diarist, has a surname pronounced 'peeps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Pepys is the most famous English diarist, so a diarist is an example definition.

clue.text: Look! There's a mouse by piano!

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
eek is the cartoon shriek of someone who has just spotted a mouse

explanation.surface: Someone screams at a rodent scurrying beside the piano.
explanation.definitionFit: To peek is to take a quick look, so the imperative 'Look!' is a synonym.

clue.text: Vagabond's precipitate movement

definitions.note: as an adjective vagabond means roving or wandering

indicators.note: movement of the letters means they are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: A tramp makes a sudden, hasty move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movement' looks like a noun the tramp makes, but it signals rearranging PRECIPITATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A wandering, roving life is a travelling one moving from place to place, so the adjectival vagabond is a synonym.

clue.text: Guard started to cross lake

indicators.note: to cross means the first piece goes across the second, holding it inside

parts.note: a horse that started in alarm shied
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A sentry set off to go over a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: To shield something is to protect it, so guard as a verb is a synonym.

clue.text: Billie occasionally visiting dealer in Bloomsbury perhaps

indicators.note: visiting means these letters drop in and sit inside the other piece

parts.note: a pusher is a drug dealer

indicators.note: occasionally means only some of the letters of Billie are taken, every other one

explanation.surface: A woman called Billie sometimes calls on a drug dealer in a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'occasionally' takes B, L, I from Billie, which go inside PUSHER. Bloomsbury looks like the London district but is the firm Bloomsbury Publishing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloomsbury Publishing, which issued the Harry Potter books, is an example of a book company.

clue.text: Ready to drop? This might help

definitions.text: Ready to drop? This might help

parts.words: Ready to drop? This might help
parts.note: ready to drop suggests exhaustion, but a skydiver about to drop from a plane needs this canopy

explanation.surface: Someone worn out is offered a remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready to drop' reads as exhausted; here it means about to jump from an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A skydiver or paratrooper relies on this canopy to fall safely from an aircraft.

clue.text: Where one on drugs might go for kicks?

definitions.text: Where one on drugs might go for kicks?

parts.words: Where one on drugs might go for kicks?
parts.note: A big British pharmacy chain where prescriptions are filled; footwear is also what you kick with

explanation.surface: A question about where a drug-taker seeks thrills.
explanation.walkthrough: Boots is a British high-street chemist; someone on medication goes there, and kicks are delivered with footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: The chemist chain suits a person on medication, while footwear is what delivers kicks.

clue.text: Reporter's local group conspiring

indicators.note: a reporter speaking the word means it is judged by how it sounds

parts.note: a local is a pub, an inn
a league is a group of clubs or allies

explanation.surface: A journalist's neighbourhood association is plotting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'local' is British for one's neighbourhood pub; INN said aloud gives IN.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in league with someone is to be in secret alliance, plotting together.

clue.text: Dynasty's influence failing in the end

indicators.note: failing in the end means the last letter of the word gives out and is lost

parts.note: having a hand in something means having influence over it

explanation.surface: A ruling family's power fades at last.
explanation.definitionFit: The Han ruled China for about four centuries, an example of an imperial ruling house.

clue.text: In some homes it's a problem of course

definitions.text: In some homes it's a problem of course

parts.words: In some homes it's a problem of course
parts.note: of course looks like 'naturally', but means a damp-proof course in a wall, whose failure lets moisture creep up

explanation.surface: A remark that some households naturally have troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: A damp-proof course is a waterproof layer in a wall; when it fails, moisture climbs from the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Moisture seeping upward through brickwork from the ground is a common household building defect.

clue.text: Previously more like a man of noble birth

definitions.meaning: previously means at a sooner time

definitions.text: more like a man of noble birth
definitions.meaning: read playfully as the comparative of earl, a nobleman: more earl-like

explanation.surface: Once, someone was more aristocratic.
explanation.definitionFit: Sooner in time is the plain sense; the jokey second sense treats it as a comparative of the noble title earl.

clue.text: Old boys harbouring desire for figures such as these?

indicators.note: harbouring means sheltering something within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil; OBS is the plural
to long is to desire

explanation.surface: Former pupils nurse a yearning for numbers like these.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblong is a rectangle longer than it is wide, a geometric shape or figure.

clue.text: A busy place?

parts.note: busy is British slang for a police officer, so a place for busies is where officers are based

explanation.walkthrough: 'busy' looks like an adjective meaning bustling, but in British slang a busy is a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The building where police officers are based is literally a place of busies in slang.

clue.text: Incinerate husband perhaps? He's got it coming!

definitions.text: Incinerate husband perhaps? He's got it coming!

indicators.note: perhaps hints that these letters might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A wife considers burning her husband, who supposedly deserves it.
explanation.walkthrough: Whole-clue reading: kill off a husband and an estate passes on; 'He's got it coming' fits both an heir and a doomed spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate passed on after a death is what a widow or heir has coming to them.

clue.text: Exotic pastries I originally enjoyed here

indicators.note: exotic means foreign and unusual, so these letters take an unfamiliar new order
originally means only the opening letter of the following word is taken

explanation.surface: Someone recalls savouring unusual cakes at a particular spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exotic' rearranges PASTRIES to PATISSER; 'originally' gives the E of enjoyed. 'here' is where the pastries were enjoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cake shop is the place where such pastries are sold and eaten, so 'here' points to it.

clue.text: Pretentious Penny booted out by Tories for one

indicators.note: booted out means this letter is expelled from the word

parts.note: the Tories are one example of a political party

explanation.surface: A showy woman called Penny is expelled by the Conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: Tories are members of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Showily artistic in a pretentious way is the sense of the informal adjective.

clue.text: A Parisian off his head — or in perfect shape?

parts.note: un is French for a, as a Parisian would say it
touched means slightly mad, off one's head

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is either mad or in excellent condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something never handled or damaged remains pristine, in perfect condition.

clue.text: Reference work ambassador's placed in house

indicators.note: placed in means this piece is put inside the other

parts.note: Taurus is one of the astrological houses or signs of the zodiac
HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador; with the 's it gives HES

explanation.surface: A diplomat lodges a book in his home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' is the astrological sense, a sign of the zodiac such as Taurus.
explanation.definitionFit: A book listing synonyms is a standard reference book for writers.

clue.text: Child's hero under pressure to become a man of God

indicators.note: in a down answer, under means the second piece sits below the first

parts.note: Jack Reacher is the hero of Lee Child's thriller novels

explanation.surface: A boy's idol is pushed into becoming a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child' looks like any youngster but is the novelist Lee Child.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who delivers sermons is a minister, a churchman.

clue.text: Meddle in current rent-free arrangement

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current

indicators.note: an arrangement of the letters means they are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone sticks their nose into a deal letting a tenant live without paying.
explanation.definitionFit: To meddle is to involve oneself where one is not wanted, a synonym.

clue.text: Press knocking back the brandy

indicators.note: knocking back reads as drinking, but signals that the word runs backwards

parts.note: marc is a brandy distilled from grape pressings

explanation.surface: Journalists are downing spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking back' looks like drinking the brandy, which fits the surface, but it turns MARC round.
explanation.definitionFit: To press things together tightly is to pack or stuff them, a synonym.

clue.text: Lorry carrying Charlie's very cold

indicators.note: carrying means the first piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: artic is British slang for an articulated lorry
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A truck transporting a man is freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: A lorry is a British truck; an artic is a large one with a pivoting trailer.
explanation.definitionFit: Polar conditions are bitterly cold, so the adjective means freezing.

clue.text: Down with the same bug as Polly?

definitions.text: Down with the same bug as Polly?

parts.words: Down with the same bug as Polly?
parts.note: Polly is the stock name for a pet parrot, so being ill with its bug is the British idiom for being bitterly disappointed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Polly' is the traditional name for a parrot; the British idiom means very disappointed, but is read literally as ill.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for bitter disappointment is taken literally as ill like a pet bird.

clue.text: Attraction of girl from the south

indicators.note: in a down answer, reading from the south means from the bottom up, so the word is reversed

parts.note: Tessa is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman from a southern region is appealing.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful or appealing quality, so an attraction is a synonym.

clue.text: Leading man a little lecherous

indicators.note: a little means only a small part of the word is taken, buried within it

explanation.surface: The star of a film is slightly lewd.
explanation.definitionFit: The main male character in a film or story is its protagonist.

clue.text: Estates controlled most of the game

parts.note: someone who ran a business controlled it

indicators.note: most of means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: chess is the game

explanation.surface: Landholdings dominated most of the hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Large farms with land and livestock are estates in the agricultural sense.

clue.text: Tip vessel over

indicators.note: over, in a down answer, means the word is turned upside down and read backwards

parts.note: a pan is a cooking vessel

explanation.surface: An instruction to upend a container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like the verb to upend; it is a racing tip, the nap being a tipster's most confident pick.
explanation.definitionFit: In horse racing a nap is a tipster's strongest selection of the day.

clue.text: Followers of Her Majesty holding couple back

indicators.note: back means the whole assembled string is read in reverse
holding means the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen
to couple is to join or unite

explanation.surface: The Queen's attendants are keeping a pair behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the whole container, not just the couple, which is the trap: reversing only UNITE gives nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants accompanying an important person.

clue.text: River pasture he cultivated

indicators.note: cultivated land is turned over and worked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A farmer tilled grassland by a waterway.
explanation.definitionFit: The Euphrates is a major river of Mesopotamia, an example of the class.

clue.text: I believe in Latin, as almost all the boys do

indicators.note: almost means the word stops just short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a crew is the whole gang, all the boys together

explanation.surface: A Latin phrase of faith shared by nearly every lad.
explanation.definitionFit: Credo is Latin for the first-person verb of faith, and names a statement of belief.
